Notes: c. 100 BCE: Hooper Museum (Carleton Univ.) Caesarea chronology: 'Ptolemy Lathyrus helps Jannaeus add Straton's Tower to his Judean kingdom' after the town under the tyrant Zoilus had withstood a siege by Alexander Jannaeus. Year Established = -100 (c.): Hasmonean (Jewish) annexation of Strato's Tower is the earliest documented Jewish presence/control at the site; date of the conquest is disputed (c. 103/100, 96 or 90 BCE in other sources). No count.

Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Caesarea' (M. Avi-Yonah): 'In 96 b.c.e. Alexander Yannai captured the city' and it remained part of the Hasmonean kingdom until Pompey restored it as an autonomous city (63 BCE). Hasmonean conquest; no count of Jewish residents.

Wikipedia (citing Roller & Hohlfelder, BASOR 1983): in 90 BCE Alexander Jannaeus captured Straton's Tower; it was enlarged under Hasmonean rule 'becoming a Jewish village' and 'remained a Jewish settlement for two more generations' until Roman annexation. Presence of a Jewish settlement; no count. (Wikipedia used as last resort; original article not accessed.)

Holum & Raban, NEAEHL (Stern ed. 1993) as quoted on this page: 'During forty years of Hasmonean rule, Straton's Tower probably acquired a Jewish population', though the rabbis excluded the town itself (not its territory) from the borders of the Land (Tosefta Shevi'it 4:11). Year = midpoint of Hasmonean rule c. 103-63 BCE. Probable (not certain) Jewish settlement; no count.

Josephus, Antiquities 13.395 (Whiston): 'Now at this time the Jews were in possession of the following cities... At the sea-side, Strato's Tower, Apollonia, Joppa...'. Context: after Jannaeus's campaigns against Gamala etc. (c. 83-80 BCE), year = c. midpoint. Jewish (Hasmonean) possession of the town; no count of Jewish residents.

Josephus, Antiquities 14.76: Pompey left Strato's Tower and the other maritime cities 'in a state of freedom' and joined them to the province of Syria - end of Hasmonean (Jewish) rule over the town. Fate of any Jewish residents not stated (Population blank, not 0).

c. 10 BCE (Herod built Caesarea 22-10/9 BCE): Holum & Raban (NEAEHL 1993) as quoted on this page: 'Herod appears to have resettled the site with Jews as well as with Greek-speaking pagans.' Herodian re-foundation with a Jewish component of the population; no count.

Early Roman period (63 BCE-70 CE; midpoint 4, c.): Lee I. Levine, 'The Jewish Community at Caesarea in Late Antiquity' (Caesarea Papers, JRA Suppl. 5, 1992): 'Though built as a Greek city, it housed a large and powerful Jewish community, and was first ruled by a king who was Jewish' (Herod); refers to the struggle between Jews and pagans in the first century. Large organized community; no number given.

Josephus, Antiquities 19.343-352: King Agrippa I (Jewish king; Judea, Samaria and Caesarea added to his realm under Claudius) held games at Caesarea and died there 'in the seventh year of his reign' (44 CE). Presence of the Jewish king and court; not a population figure.

1st c. CE (midpoint 50): Encyclopaedia Judaica (Avi-Yonah): 'The population of Caesarea was half gentile and half Jewish'; the divergent claims of the two groups to citizenship and municipal rights led to frequent disputes that finally sparked the war of 66 CE. Proportion only, no count (Population blank).

c. 57 CE (Paul's last journey to Jerusalem): Acts 21:8-10 - Paul's party stayed 'in the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the seven' at Caesarea, who had four prophesying daughters (Acts 8:40 already brings Philip to Caesarea c. 35 CE). Philip was a Hellenist Jewish follower of Jesus: a Jewish(-Christian) household resident in Caesarea; individual presence, no count.

c. 59 CE (dating per Harland, under Felix): Josephus, War 2.266-270 (Thackeray/Marcus trans. adapted by P. Harland): 'Another disturbance occurred at Caesarea, where the Judean portion of the population rose against the Syrian inhabitants'; Judeans claimed the city because its founder Herod was a Judean; the quarrel led to armed clashes and Felix sent troops against Judean crowds - 'Many were killed'. Evidence of a sizeable Jewish population (no count); casualties not counted.

c. 60 CE (after Festus replaced Felix): Josephus, Antiquities 20.173-184: dispute between the Jews and Syrians of Caesarea over equal civic rights; the Jews were superior in wealth; the Syrians argued the city had been Strato's Tower with no Jewish inhabitant then (a partisan claim, not evidence of absence); 'the principal of the Jewish inhabitants of Caesarea went up to Rome to accuse Felix'; two Syrians bribed Burrhus to obtain an imperial letter 'to disannul that equality of the Jewish privileges of citizens' - loss of Jewish civic equality. No count.

1906 Jewish Encyclopedia 'Caesarea': Jews lived there from the Maccabean period and grew in number, with 'frequent quarrels resulting between pagans and Jews'; 'sanguinary conflicts under the administration of Felix'; 'in the year 61 Nero declared the pagans to be the sole rulers' of the city. Event affecting the community; no count.

May 66 CE (Nero yr 12, month Artemisius): Josephus, War 2.284-292: the Jews of Caesarea had a synagogue adjoining a Greek's property; workshops blocked access; leaders with John the publican bribed Florus with 8 talents; a Greek sacrificed birds at the synagogue entrance on the Sabbath; after fighting the Jews took their 'books of the law' and withdrew to Narbata, 60 stadia away; John and 12 leading men imprisoned by Florus. Organized community with a synagogue and leadership; no count.

Summer 66 CE: Josephus, War 2.457 (Thackeray/Marcus trans. adapted by Harland): the Caesareans massacred their Judean residents - 'Within one hour more than twenty thousand were slaughtered' and 'Caesarea was completely emptied of Judeans because the fugitives were arrested by orders of Florus' (sent in chains to the dockyards). Population 0 = documented absence per Josephus. The 20,000 is an ancient death-toll figure (Harland calls these accounts 'tendentious'), not a resident count; left out of Population.

Holum & Raban (NEAEHL 1993) as quoted on this page: 'In 66 CE, on the eve of the First Jewish Revolt against Rome, the pagan majority massacred most of Caesarea's Jews (War II, 457)' - modern scholars say 'most', not all; Population left blank for this source. Also characterizes the pagans as the majority.

67 CE (Panemus): Josephus, War 3.409-413: Caesarea 'a very great city of Judea' inhabited mostly by Greeks, who welcomed Vespasian out of 'the hatred they bore to those that were conquered' and demanded Josephus's execution. Hostile gentile majority after the 66 massacre; no Jewish residents mentioned.

Autumn 70 CE: Josephus, War 7.20, 7.36-38: Titus kept the Jewish captives from Jerusalem and his spoils at Caesarea by the sea; Simon bar Giora brought there in chains; at games for Domitian's birthday the captives slain 'exceeded two thousand five hundred'. Captives and death toll, not residents (left out of Population).

Vespasian's reign 69-79 CE (midpoint 74, c.): J. Patrich (Bible and Interpretation, 2011), citing Malalas: Vespasian converted a Jewish synagogue at Caesarea into an odeum. Post-revolt confiscation of a community building; no count.
